newsitem.title: CANADA: Panel recommends Canada Post sell courier service.
newsitem.headline: Panel recommends Canada Post sell courier service.

text.p: A government-appointed review board recommended on Tuesday that the government's Canada Post sell its Purolator Courier service and get out of the courier business altogether.
To compensate, it recommended that courier services attach a first class stamp to each courier shipment, thus contributing revenue to Canada Post.
It recommended: "That the government specifically divest itself of Purolator Courier at fair market value and to withdraw from all other courier services."

It added: "That, in exchange for Canada Post Corporation's withdrawal from competition in the courier market, the courier industry be required to make a compensatory contribution to the corporation's revenues, in the form of a requirement that all courier shipments must have affixed to them a first-class postage stamp."
The committee also recommended that first-class postage rise to 50 Canadian cents from the present 45 cents.
Canadian Public Works and Government Services Minister Diane Marleau immediately rejected the central recommendations at least for now.

"The government is not prepared, at this time, to accept the recommendation for withdrawal from courier services. Accordingly, Purolator Courier is not for sale," she told a news conference as she unveiled the recommendations.

"I am not prepared to accept the recommendations for an increase in the price of first-class postage, or to impose levies on couriers or ad-mail," she said, adding the government did not want to add to Canadians' financial burdens.
But she said she has selected TD Securities Inc to assess the impact of the recommendations on Canada Post's ability to remain financially self-sustaining.
She said that in one area, the government would move quickly -- namely to withdraw from the delivery of junk mail, or "economy unaddressed ad-mail," where alternate capability exists.
Marleau said she had asked Canada Post to exit from the junk mail business in a way that minimizes disruption for the large number of Canadians it employed in that sector.
She has also asked Canada Post to examine the feasibility and potential impact of also withdrawing from the delivery of premium unaddressed ad-mail, a news release said.
In November 1995, the government formed the review board and gave it free rein in making recommendations after hearing from businesses, citizens and experts.
Marleau expects the TD financial analysis to be completed by December and to go to cabinet with her recommendations early next year.
Among the commercial couriers operating in Canada are Federal Express Corp, United Parcel Service and DHL Worldwide Express.
